CRA describes two separate ways a mutual fund in a non-registered account is taxed. While you own the units, the distributions the fund pays are taxable each year, even when they are reinvested in more units. When you sell or redeem units, you are taxed on the gain, if any, usually as a capital gain. A redemption therefore has three parts: your own cost coming back, which is not taxed; half of the gain, which is left out of income; and the other half of the gain, which is taxed at your marginal rate.

Contributions into a TFSA or RRSP use room that is not otherwise used, and growth inside those accounts is not taxed while it stays there; pausing does not normally lose the room, which carries forward, but cash parked outside the account earns taxable interest. In a non-registered account, every month’s purchase adds to the adjusted cost base, and units bought near the low carry larger future gains, which are taxed only when units are sold. The fund itself does not change its tax treatment; the account’s rules decide it.

Contributions made during a fall buy more units, so an account fed from pay can be back above its contributions well before the market regains its old peak. Pausing in cash avoids buying into further losses, but if a recovery comes, it waits for prices to return before buying. Neither choice makes a recovery happen, and money you may need soon should not be in the fund at all.

The OSC cautions that diversification provides reasonable protection in normal markets but can be less effective in extreme conditions, when most investments fall together, and warns against selling in a downturn. Redeeming fund units in a non-registered account is not fully taxed: part of each withdrawal returns your own cost, and only half of the gain is taxable. That makes early withdrawals light on tax. As withdrawals continue and the fund grows, the cost base shrinks and the taxable share rises, while reinvested distributions are taxed every year whether or not any units are sold.

Redemptions remove cost base in proportion to value; reinvested distributions add to it. The gap between the two lines is unrealized gain. It is taxed when units are sold or are considered sold (a deemed disposition), so deferral postpones the tax; it does not cancel it.

Someone who invests a fixed amount from every paycheque into a balanced or equity fund will, sooner or later, open a statement showing that the account is worth less than the money put in. A common reaction is to stop the automatic contribution and keep the money in savings “until things settle down”. It feels like the cautious choice: why buy more of something that is falling?

That has practical consequences. Keeping a careful ACB record matters, because without one an investor may overpay by treating too much of a redemption as gain; the reinvested-distributions guide shows how reinvestments and returns of capital change it. Distributions are taxed every year even when nothing is sold, which is one reason the asset-location guide places the most heavily taxed income in registered accounts where room allows.

The 29.65% default is the 2026 federal rate of 20.5% plus Ontario’s 9.15%, which together apply to taxable income between about CAD 58,523 and CAD 107,785 in 2026 according to CRA’s rate tables. Your rate depends on your income and province, so change the two inputs; Ontario’s surtax, credits and income-tested benefits are not modeled.

The case for continuing rests on contributions that can stay invested for many years. Pausing, or redirecting, can be the right call when the reason is your own cash flow rather than the market:

The comparison plan stops buying in month 1, holds every contribution in cash earning 2.5% a year, invests all of that cash in one purchase in month 60 when prices are back at the old peak, and then resumes the monthly contribution. Both plans put in exactly the same money: CAD 50,000 by month 60 and CAD 68,000 by month 96.

The default fund is worth CAD 300,000 and has an adjusted cost base (ACB) of CAD 200,000: the total paid for the units, including reinvested distributions. The investor redeems CAD 18,000 at the start of the year.

The default scenario starts with CAD 20,000 already invested at a market peak and adds CAD 500 at each month-end. The market falls 35% over 18 months, so the price at the low is 65% of the old peak. It then takes 42 more months to climb back, regaining the old peak in month 60, and grows 6% a year afterwards. Each phase moves by the same percentage every month, a smooth shape chosen so that each effect can be seen; real markets move in jumps and false starts.

The first chart compares the tax on the same CAD 18,000 at the same 29.65% rate. A TFSA withdrawal is not taxed. Non-registered units bought recently, with a cost near their value, produce almost no gain. With the entered cost base the tax is CAD 889.50. If the units had no cost base left, the whole CAD 18,000 would be gain and the tax would be CAD 2,668.50. An RRSP or RRIF withdrawal is fully taxable, CAD 5,337 at this rate.

The first chart plots both account values against the money put in. At the low in month 18, the continued plan is worth about CAD 20,400 against CAD 29,000 contributed; the paused plan is worth about CAD 22,159, because the CAD 9,000 held in cash did not fall. This is the stretch that makes pausing feel right.
The first year, step by step

The fund also pays distributions of 1.5% a year on the remaining CAD 282,000, CAD 4,230, which are reinvested. The model taxes them at the full marginal rate, CAD 1,254.20, which is conservative: distributions of eligible dividends or capital gains would be taxed less, as the fund income-type guide shows. After both amounts, about CAD 15,856 of the CAD 18,000 is left to spend if the tax is paid from it.
The fund itself has no special tax status; a fund held in a TFSA or RRSP follows that account’s rules instead. This guide is about the non-registered case.

The fund starts at $300,000 with an adjusted cost base of $200,000. $18,000 is redeemed at the start of the first year, rising 2% a year. Each redemption uses the average cost per unit, so only the part above cost is a capital gain, and half of that gain is taxed at the combined 29.65% marginal rate (20.5% federal plus 9.15% provincial or territorial). Units then grow 4% a year and distributions of 1.5% a year are reinvested and taxed at the full marginal rate, a conservative simplification: eligible dividends and capital gains distributions would be taxed less. Tax is paid from the redeemed cash. Returns are hypothetical, not a forecast, and this is not a personal tax calculation.

The fund still holds about CAD 98,468 at the end, with an ACB of about CAD 40,150. The tax on that unrealized gain, about CAD 8,646 at the same rate, has been deferred, not avoided: gains are taxed when units are sold or are considered to be sold (a deemed disposition). The gain-timing guide values what deferral is worth. Extend the plan to 25 years and the default fund runs out in year 24: lower tax does not make a withdrawal rate sustainable.

The heatmap repeats the break-even month for different fall sizes and starting balances, keeping the 60-month round trip. Two patterns stand out. With no starting balance, the account is back above its contributions by month 32 or 33 whatever the depth of the fall, because a deeper fall also means cheaper units. With a starting balance of 240 monthly contributions, CAD 120,000 here, break-even moves out to month 55 or 56: a large existing balance follows the market, and new contributions are too small to pull the average down much. The earlier in a saving life a crash happens, the more the contributions dominate.

The heatmap reruns the 20-year plan for starting cost bases from 100% to 0% of value and unit growth from 0% to 8% a year. A fund bought recently with no growth pays about 3.2% of its withdrawals in tax, all of it on distributions. A fund with no cost base left that grows 8% a year pays about 21.7%. In between, the starting ACB sets the level and growth sets the slope.

The market regains its old peak in month 60. With contributions continued, the account is back above the money put in by month 46, 14 months earlier. The larger the starting balance compared with each contribution, the closer the account follows the market line.
The month the statement turns red

The picture changes on the way back up. In month 60, when the market is exactly at its old peak, the continued plan is worth about CAD 57,500, while the paused plan is worth about CAD 51,898 after investing its cash at the peak price. By month 96 the values are about CAD 88,104 and CAD 81,432. The gap of roughly CAD 6,672 comes from the units that the monthly contributions bought below the old peak, less the interest the paused cash earned.

The reason is the average price. The 60 contributions made until the peak returned bought their units at an average price of about 80% of the old peak. FINRA describes this as a benefit of regular investing in a decline: a fixed amount buys more units when prices are lower. The same page sets out the limits: holding cash and spreading purchases out often produces lower returns than investing at once, especially over longer periods, and per-transaction fees can erode returns.

The recovery length is the decisive assumption, and it is the one nobody knows in advance. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor site notes that markets have historically recovered from declines but that this can take months or several years. Change the inputs to try a faster bounce, a slower climb, or a recovery that does not arrive within the horizon.
The same withdrawal from different accounts

The second and third charts follow the plan for 20 years, with the withdrawal rising 2% a year and units growing 4% a year after fund costs. Each redemption removes cost base in proportion to value, and growth adds value but not cost. Reinvested distributions add to both. Over time the ACB falls behind the market value, so each dollar redeemed carries less cost and more gain.

The second chart compares two ratios: the market price as a share of the old peak, and the account value as a share of the money put in. With contributions continued, the account is back above its contributions in month 46, 14 months before the market regains its peak. At that point the market price is still about 13% below the peak. The paused plan crosses in month 53, helped by its cash interest and by the partial recovery of its starting balance.
The taxable share grows as the fund’s gain grows relative to its cost base. In year 1, 33.3% of the redemption is gain; by year 20 it is 58.5%.

The third chart values each year’s block of purchases at the old peak price in month 60. Contributions made in months 13 to 24, around the low, show a paper gain of about 46.7%. Contributions in the first year of the fall show about 17.2%, and those made in the last year before the peak returned show only about 5.9%. The starting balance, bought at the peak, shows nothing.

These are the purchases that a pause skips. They also show why a pause is hard to undo in practice: the months that turned out best were the months when statements looked worst, and an investor waiting for “things to settle down” usually restarts after prices have risen. The waiting-for-a-dip guide tests the opposite habit, holding new money back until prices fall, and finds the same difficulty from the other side.

Deciding whether to sell what is already invested is different again, and is tested in the exit-and-re-entry guide.

Two cautions keep this from being a ranking of accounts. The RRSP contributions were deducted from income when they were made, so taxing the withdrawal completes a deal that began with a refund; the RRSP and TFSA timing guide compares the full cycle. And the RRSP cash flow differs: for a lump-sum withdrawal, CRA says the institution withholds tax at source, 30% outside Quebec on an amount over CAD 15,000, which may be more or less than the final tax, as the withholding guide explains. Non-registered redemptions have no such withholding, so the tax is settled with the return or through instalments.
